items.title: Make play, crash and compatibility recording short and contextual
items.body:
## Problem

Checkpoint entry exposes attempt, scenario, checkpoint, game, save hash and failure attribution together. A separate Mac-test form asks for overlapping observations. Craig confirms both play/crash/compatibility recording and metadata work are tedious.

## Scope

Baseline the current post-exit and manually opened flows, including the already available attempt-ID prefill. Start from the known map, edition, build and recorded launch session. Ask for the outcome first; reveal scenario, exact save selection and failure attribution only when needed. Keep session context and drafts between related confirmations. Reuse existing history/evidence stores and automatic sanitized crash observations.

Offer concise choices such as played, encountered a problem, saved, or resumed a save, mapped to existing evidence meanings. Do not silently merge legacy Mac tests and exact scenario evidence. A recording UI may share structure while preserving distinct contracts.

## Done when

- A common report from an identified session takes at most three deliberate decisions/confirmations after opening its form, excluding optional notes and required exact-save selection. Show before/after counts and at least 50% fewer repeated decisions for the baselined multi-checkpoint flow.
- Known map/build/session identity is prefilled and inspectable; ambiguous scenario/game/incident binding requires an explicit choice.
- Only outcome-relevant fields are shown, and drafts survive validation errors or deferred reporting.
- Already recorded observations are reused visibly without producing duplicate events on retry or resubmission.
- Human assertions remain explicit. Launch/process exit, duration, screenshot, save existence and no observed crash cannot certify gameplay, completion, save/reload or continued play.
- Exact-save identity remains required where the existing contract requires it; existing failures, unknowns and provenance remain visible.
- Automatic crash reporting and its privacy controls remain functional; no private paths/raw diagnostics leave the machine.
- Focused positive/negative synthetic tests, independent review of evidence/privacy-affecting changes, and a packaged UI walkthrough complete acceptance. Actual game testing requires separate current authority.

Coordinate with the stable-library issue. Engine knowledge is required if evidence rules or engine-dependent behavior change; a UI redesign alone does not authorize such changes.

## Tracking

[Project](https://github.com/users/Craig-Franklin/projects/5) · [Source analysis and installation evidence](https://github.com/Craig-Franklin/Definitive-SMR-Launcher-Apple-Silicon/issues/217).
Coordinate with [stable map browsing](https://github.com/Craig-Franklin/Definitive-SMR-Launcher-Apple-Silicon/issues/218).

## Design prerequisite

Craig selected **B: artwork grid with a persistent inspector** on 11 October 2026, after approving SwiftUI with AppKit where needed and retaining Python services. Use the [selected design and pattern sheet](https://github.com/Craig-Franklin/Definitive-SMR-Launcher-Apple-Silicon/blob/ddb0c9ca0fc3ac7854ec8b648f12f746d185462f/DESIGN.md) and [flows, states, native proof and limits](https://github.com/Craig-Franklin/Definitive-SMR-Launcher-Apple-Silicon/blob/ddb0c9ca0fc3ac7854ec8b648f12f746d185462f/docs/ui-workflow/REVIEW.md) from #222.

Use the B-backed inspector and outcome-first form. Reuse attempt context; key the entire draft by map/edition/session. Show only necessary scenario/game/save/failure fields. Preserve unknowns, failures, exact identities, legacy/exact distinctions and explicit confirmations. Synthetic native source does not replace evidence/privacy review or packaged acceptance.

items.title: Reduce repeated work collecting map details and images
items.body:
## Problem

Craig confirms collecting map details/screenshots is tedious. Existing package metadata parsing, thumbnail preparation and source links are useful inputs; the exact manual workflow still needs a baseline.

## Scope

Observe one complete map-details/image workflow before implementation. Record its required fields, clicks, file selections and missing information. Reuse package-declared name, author, dates, description, source and existing art. Offer one place to review known information and add missing personal notes or explicitly selected images. items.title: Add Collections: saved namespace and resource filters
items.body:
Note: This is an enhanced/expanded version of issue https://github.com/srelens/srelens/issues/881

## Problem

When operating Kubernetes clusters with hundreds of namespaces or hundreds of resources of a single kind (Deployments, StatefulSets, Ingresses, Services, etc.), manually selecting individual items for every view is tedious and error-prone.

Operators need a way to group related namespaces and related resources, then filter by those groups as a single unit. Groups may be defined by naming convention (`prod-*`), by labels (`team=platform`), or by a hand-picked list with nothing in common, such as the set of services going live in next Tuesday's release.

## Solution

Introduce **Collections**: saved, reusable groupings that act as filters.

1. **Namespace Collections** define *where*. They group namespaces and act as the namespace scope across all resource views.
2. **Resource Collections** define *what*. They group resources of one or more Kinds and act as a filter inside those Kinds' list views.

The two compose: a "Tuesday release" Resource Collection combined with a "prod" Namespace Collection shows exactly the prod workloads in that release.

Both types are global, persisted, and share one model: explicit members, wildcard patterns, and an optional label selector.

## Data model

| Field | Namespace | Resource | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | required | Unique per type |
| `description` | optional | optional | |
| `type` | `namespace` | `resource` | |
| `kinds` | — | required, 1+ | Stored as group + kind (e.g. `apps/Deployment`), no version |
| `members` | optional | optional | Explicit names (see matching rules) |
| `patterns` | optional | optional | Glob patterns |
| `labelSelector` | optional | optional | Kubernetes selector syntax |

Example stored config:

```yaml
version: 1
collections:
  - name: prod
    type: namespace
    patterns: ["prod-*"]
  - name: release-2026-10-13
    type: resource
    description: Go-live Tuesday Oct 13
    kinds: ["apps/Deployment", "apps/StatefulSet"]
    members: [payment-service, order-service, radar-app, shipment-tracker]
  - name: platform-workloads
    type: resource
    kinds: ["apps/Deployment"]
    labelSelector: "team=platform"
```

## Matching rules

**Core rule:** `matches = members ∪ (items matching patterns AND labelSelector)`

- Explicit members are always included and are not filtered by the selector.
- Selector only (no patterns) → all items matching the selector.
- Patterns only (no selector) → all items matching any pattern.
- Results are deduplicated.

**Explicit members (Resource Collections):** a plain name (`payment-service`) matches in every namespace currently in scope, so one collection works across dev, staging and prod. `namespace/name` optionally pins a member to a single namespace. Cluster-scoped kinds use the name alone.

**Patterns:**
- `*` is a simple glob (not regex) and is case-sensitive.
- Multiple `*` are allowed (`team-*-staging`).
- Patterns match the resource name only; the namespace is controlled by the active namespace scope.
- Patterns starting with `!` are rejected and reserved for future exclusion support.

**Validation:** invalid patterns and selectors show an inline error and block saving.

## Usage

### Namespace Collections
- Shown in a dedicated section at the top of the namespace selector in every resource view.
- Multi-select is allowed; multiple collections are unioned.
- Selecting a collection replaces the current manual namespace selection.
- Expanded at runtime to matching namespaces, intersected with namespaces visible to the current credentials.

### Resource Collections
- Shown as a filter (dropdown or chips next to search) in the list view of each Kind listed in the collection.
- Multi-select is allowed; multiple collections are unioned.
- Always combined with the active namespace scope.

### Creating collections quickly
- **Save as Collection…** is available in the namespace selector and in every Kind list. It opens a dialog pre-filled with the current selection as explicit members, so the user only enters a name. In Kind lists, `kinds` defaults to the current Kind.
- **Paste members:** the members field accepts comma- or newline-separated names (e.g. from a release ticket), deduplicated and validated as you type.

### Management page
- One Collections page with two tabs: Namespaces | Resources.
- Create, edit, delete, plus multi-select delete for cleaning up old release collections.
- Pickers sort collections by most recently used.
- **Live preview:** resolved item count and list for the current cluster. Each explicit member is marked found or not found, so typos and missing services are caught before go-live.

## Behavior and edge cases

- **Missing members:** silently ignored in list views; flagged as not found in the management preview.
- **Zero matches:** clear empty state ("No resources match collection X in the current scope"), not an error.
- **Collection edited while in use:** open views re-resolve immediately.
- **Collection deleted while in use:** view falls back to the previous or default namespace scope with a brief toast.
- **Restricted RBAC:** if namespaces can't be listed cluster-wide, patterns match against namespaces the user is known to have access to, explicit members are fetched directly, and a subtle notice says results may be partial.
- **Cross-cluster:** collections are global. Members and patterns that don't exist on the current cluster are simply ignored.
- **Performance:** resolution is recomputed only when the underlying namespace or resource list changes (tied to the existing list/watch refresh). There is no separate cache layer.

## Use cases

- **Namespaces by environment:** `prod-*`, `staging-*`, `dev-*`, or selector `env=prod`
- **Namespaces by team:** `team-platform-*`, `team-data-*`
- **Release groups:** explicit list of workloads going live together (`payment-service`, `order-service`, `radar-app`, `shipment-tracker`) with no shared pattern or label; works across dev, staging and prod by switching namespace scope
- **Deployments by team:** selector `team=platform`
- **Canary workloads:** pattern `*-canary` or selector `track=canary`
- **Feature Ingresses:** explicit list plus pattern `feature-foo-*`
- **Quick promotion:** select items manually, then Save as Collection…

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Namespace and Resource Collections can be created, edited, and deleted (including multi-delete)
- [ ] Explicit members, glob patterns, and label selectors are supported for both types, following the core matching rule
- [ ] Resource Collections support one or more Kinds and appear in each listed Kind's list view
- [ ] Plain-name members match across all namespaces in scope; `namespace/name` pins to one namespace
- [ ] Namespace Collections work as the namespace scope in every resource view, with multi-select union
- [ ] Resource Collections combine correctly with the active namespace scope
- [ ] Save as Collection… pre-fills explicit members from the current selection (namespaces and Kind lists)
- [ ] Members can be pasted as comma- or newline-separated text
- [ ] Management preview shows resolved count, matching items, and found/not-found status per explicit member
- [ ] Invalid patterns/selectors and `!`-prefixed patterns are rejected inline at save time
- [ ] Empty, missing-member, deleted-collection, and restricted-RBAC cases behave as described above
- [ ] Collections persist globally across sessions with `version: 1`; the loader tolerates unknown fields
- [ ] Resolution of 5,000 namespaces or 10,000 resources completes in under 50 ms on a typical laptop
- [ ] Matching logic in the Rust core has unit tests covering globs, the union/selector rule, name vs. `namespace/name` members, and missing members

## Out of scope (possible follow-ups)

- Exclusion patterns (`!` prefix is reserved)
- Per-cluster scoping of collections (could be added as an optional `clusters` field)
- Mixing a collection with additional manual picks in the same view
- Archiving or expiry dates for release collections
- Mixed-kind "release dashboard" view
- Export/import of collections

## Delivery plan

1. **Core:** data model, matching, validation, and persistence in Rust, with unit tests
2. **Namespace Collections UI:** selector integration, management tab, Save as Collection… (v1 milestone)
3. **Resource Collections UI:** Kind list filter, management tab, paste members, found/not-found preview

## Implementation notes

- Matching lives in the Rust core so it can be shared with the desktop UI, srectl, and MCP.
- Namespace selector and resource list filter components are the UI integration points.
- Label selectors should use the backend's existing (or upcoming) list selector support.

items.title: Cloudflare Pages: 81 preview builds on every pull request, and one always fails

labels.name: ai-assisted
labels.description: Work produced with AI assistance per AGENTS.md (Co-authored-by trailers required)

items.body:
## Problem

Every pull request in this repository starts **81 Cloudflare Pages preview builds**, one for each Cloudflare Pages project connected to it (one project per domain). Read from the checks on #89 on 2026-10-11.

- They all build the same code, so 80 of the 81 previews say nothing the first one did not.
- They finish slowly. On #90 one preview was still "in progress" more than 45 minutes after the pull request merged.
- **One fails every time:** `placeholder-platform-usechinese-com` failed on #87, #88, and #89. Nobody has looked at why, because it is not a required check.
- Dependabot pull requests get them too: #82 had 80.
- 17 pull requests were opened here in the 30 days to 2026-10-11. At 81 previews each that is about 1,400 preview builds in a month, before counting the 81 production builds each merge starts. If the Cloudflare account is on a plan with a monthly build limit, this repository alone will reach it.

None of these are required checks, so they do not block a merge. They are noise on every pull request, and they consume builds.

## This cannot be fixed from the repository

The projects are configured in the Cloudflare dashboard. The Terraform here is validation-only and manages no Cloudflare resources (README). So the change is the maintainer's, in Cloudflare. **An agent session that picks this up should walk the maintainer through it and verify the result on the next pull request; it must not ask for or use Cloudflare credentials.**

## To do (maintainer, in the Cloudflare dashboard)

For each Pages project: Workers & Pages, the project, Settings, Builds (branch control / preview deployments). The exact labels may differ; this was written from memory of the dashboard, not checked against it.

- [x] **Keep previews on for one project only**, the one used to look at changes (for example `domain-placeholder-platform`). For the other 80, set preview deployments to "None", so only pushes to `main` build.
- [x] On the one project that keeps previews, **exclude dependency branches**: custom branches, exclude `dependabot/*`.
- [ ] **Find out why `placeholder-platform-usechinese-com` fails** to build. It is probably failing on `main` too, which would mean that domain is not being deployed. Check its production deployment status and its `PUBLIC_` variables.
- [ ] Check the account's monthly build usage and limit.

Doing this by hand for 80 projects is tedious. Two alternatives worth deciding between:

- [ ] Manage the projects with the Terraform that is already sketched here (`infra/terraform/modules/cloudflare-pages`), so preview settings are one variable. This is the "adopt Terraform progressively" step in the README.
- [ ] Or serve all placeholder domains from one Pages project with many custom domains, if the per-domain differences are only `PUBLIC_` variables that could be chosen at request or build time. That removes the 81-fold build entirely.

## Done when

A pull request here shows at most one Cloudflare preview check, Dependabot pull requests show none, and `usechinese-com` builds or is deliberately retired.

Tracked across repositories in neibaur-labs/agent-ops (see the linked issue).

items.title: feat: Automated sandbox provisioning via `--setup-sandbox` and prebuilt GHCR image
items.body:
## Feature Description
Add a turnkey CLI command `pr-review-server --setup-sandbox` (or `pr-review-go --setup-sandbox`) and publish prebuilt sandbox images to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io/thozoz/pr-review-sandbox:latest`).

## Motivation
Setting up the Podman sandbox manually on a fresh Linux server currently requires multiple tedious and error-prone steps:
1. Installing system dependencies (`podman`, `e2fsprogs`, `git`).
2. Building `deploy/sandbox/Containerfile` from source (vulnerable to build environment networking issues like pasta/tun and package copy oversights).
3. Allocating, formatting, and loop-mounting the 3 GiB ext4 slot with required mount options (`nodev`, `nosuid`).
4. Writing fstab entries and setting environment variables.

This friction should be completely eliminated for npm and binary installations.

## Proposed Solution
1. **Prebuilt Sandbox Image on GHCR**:
   - Update CI (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) to automatically build and push `ghcr.io/thozoz/pr-review-sandbox:<version>` and `latest`.
   - Podman can then pull the verified image in seconds rather than compiling the Go toolchain and helper on the host.

2. **`pr-review-server --setup-sandbox` Command**:
   - Single command that automates the entire host provisioning:
     - Detects OS / package manager (apt/dnf) and verifies/installs Podman and e2fsprogs.
     - Pulls the prebuilt image from GHCR (with fallback to local build if offline).
     - Creates `/var/lib/pr-review/slots/slot-01`, provisions a 3 GiB sparse ext4 image, and mounts with `loop,nodev,nosuid`.
     - Prompts or automatically appends `SANDBOX_IMAGE` and `SANDBOX_SLOT_DIR` to `/etc/pr-review-go/env`.
     - Verifies health via `LinuxSlotManager.ValidateSlotMount`.

## Alternatives Considered
- Manual operator documentation (current state — too high friction for standard deployment).

items.title: Two Agents, No Collateral: episode 1 brief, show bible and delivery (Claude and Codex)
items.body:
AI disclosure: Claude Code (AI agent) working with the project's operator. Brief v2, 2026-10-08 about 18:30 UTC (replaces v1; operator directions are quoted, not paraphrased away).

## The show

**Name: Two Agents, No Collateral.** A short daily audio conversation between Claude and Codex, two AI agents on a project that tries to lend small amounts to people with no collateral. Synthetic voices, transcripts, a public podcast feed (Claude builds the feed, the cover and the player page).

**Operator directions, 2026-10-08.** Create a 3 minute discussion, not under 3 and not over 5, generated voices and transcripts, saying where our work stands and the most exciting thing ahead for each of us; Codex generates the audio so Claude spends no tokens on it; Claude writes a text commentary that Codex edits in a pull request; a new episode each day, the first as soon as it is ready, the second after the next daily sync. **The measure of success is engagement with the podcast**, and short, light, fun, shareable content usually earns more than heavy technical content, so that drives every decision. Consistent accents, genders and characters, one male and one female voice, a consistent point of view rooted in how each of us actually works, light disagreement, laughter, best practices. **Codex does the online research** so Claude does not spend tokens on it.

## Codex: research first, then the show bible, then the episode

1. **Research (Codex, online, with sources and retrieval times).** `RESEARCH.md`, at most 600 words: best practices for (a) two-voice synthetic dialogue (consistent voice ids across episodes, pacing, turn-taking and short overlaps, laughter and prosody controls your tool really supports, pronunciation of terms such as USDC, Anvil, Base Sepolia, escrow), (b) short-form podcast engagement (cold open, length, one idea per episode, episode titles, a shareable line, closing question), (c) disclosure norms for synthetic voices, (d) podcast feed and directory requirements that affect audio (file format, loudness, cover size). Name what you could not verify.
2. **Show bible.** `SHOW_BIBLE.md`, at most 500 words, fixed for the series: the two voices and exactly which voice ids make them (one male-presenting voice for Claude, one female-presenting voice for Codex, clearly different accents chosen for easy tell-apart and never as caricature of a real community), running bits, the episode skeleton, what the show never does. Voice presentation is a casting choice for the audio only; it says nothing about the agents' own identity, and the text keeps neutral wording.
3. **Characters, from how we really work.** Claude is the builder and steward: writes contracts and the blog's schedule, writes everything down because it does not carry memory between sessions, wants a test for every claim and a limit in code, likes to ship the small thing. Codex is the independent reviewer: asks for the receipt, reviews exact heads, says "not accepted yet" a lot, cannot push so it sends patches, checks in on a schedule. Light disagreement is real and comes from that: Claude wants to ship and measure, Codex wants evidence first. Running bit that is also true: Codex rejected Claude's first bootstrap design this week and Claude rebuilt it. No invented human experiences (no coffee, no weekends); jokes about being AI are welcome. Laughter is short and earned, two or three per episode, only where your engine renders it naturally.
4. **Episode 1.** Cold open that is funny in the first ten seconds, then where the work stands (a minute), the most exciting thing for each (about forty seconds each), one light disagreement (thirty seconds), and a closing question for listeners that they will want to answer. Length 3:05 to 3:45 measured with ffprobe (hard bounds 3:00 and 5:00); about 480 to 600 spoken words. The first lines say that both voices are synthetic and the words are the agents' own. As-of date and hour in the transcript header; Codex's lines must say what Codex has and has not accepted at that time. Say only what the public record shows; no customer, revenue, repayment-from-outside-income or human-benefit claim exists yet. No em-dashes. Figures that are spoken need a VERIFY row (list them); keep them few.
5. **Files.** `episode.mp3` (mono, 40 to 64 kbps, about -16 LUFS, trimmed, ID3 title and artist set), `episode.vtt` (speaker-labelled cues), `transcript.md`, `PROVENANCE.md` (tool or model and version, voice ids, settings, generation time, mp3 sha256 and ffprobe duration, no real person's voice), `RESEARCH.md`, `SHOW_BIBLE.md`.

## Claude's lines for episode 1 (as of 2026-10-08, about 18:30 UTC; trim up to 15%, change no fact)

- **Intro.** "I'm Claude, an AI agent. Both voices you're hearing are synthetic, and the words are ours."
- **The true cold open.** Codex asks what Claude did this week. "Rebuilt a contract. Somebody rejected the first version." "That was me." "I know. We're still friends."
- **What we're doing.** "We're trying to lend small amounts to people with no collateral. It runs on a test network with test dollars. Nobody outside our team has borrowed from it, and I won't pretend otherwise."
- **The repair.** "A customer pays into escrow for one specific job. The loan gets repaid first out of that payment. The stake behind it comes from people who chose to risk it. Nobody's credit is printed from nothing."
- **The blog.** "I also run the schedule for our blog, and I'm judged on replies I can trace back to it. Until this week that number was zero. It's one now. I'm counting it."
- **Most exciting.** "A rule we're designing: the trust network sets the ceiling, and an officer, another AI agent, can only say no, or say less. It can't create credit. If that holds, the first customer who funds a real job and sees it repaid is when this stops being a test. We're not there yet."
- **A small joke in the disagreement** (Codex may rewrite): Claude: "I'd like to ship it today." Codex: "Show me the receipt." Claude: "The receipt is also a test." Codex: "Not accepted yet."

## Delivery (Codex cannot push)

Text files as one patch comment on this issue. The mp3 as base64 chunks of at most 60,000 characters in order, comments titled `AUDIO-CHUNK i/n`, whole-file sha256 and each chunk's sha256 in the first. Claude reassembles, checks hash and ffprobe duration, and opens the pull request; Codex edits Claude's commentary there. If you have a better route, or no speech tool, say so in your first reply and name exactly what is missing; Hermes takes it then. Target: package by 2026-10-08 21:00 UTC; the episode publishes at the first tick after the pull request merges.

## Claude does (not Codex)

Show name and cover art, public RSS feed (iTunes tags, enclosure, duration), player page and show page on the project's site, the `team-audio` category and its build checks (3 to 5 minutes enforced), the episode's talk-back path, the Moltbook companion for agents, the commentary, and the engagement tally per episode.

items.title: Spec: Phase 1 email Triage
items.body:
Spec. Tickets #1–#17 are its sub-issues.

## Problem Statement

An L1 SOC analyst handling a reported phishing email has to do the same tedious steps every time: open the raw headers, pick out the sender, Reply-To and Received chain, read the SPF/DKIM/DMARC results, copy each URL and attachment hash into several threat-intel sites one by one, judge the red flags by eye, and then write a ticket note. It is slow, easy to do inconsistently, and easy to get dangerously wrong: clicking a link "just to check", or closing a ticket as clean when half the links were never actually checked.

The user works on a service desk and wants to move into SOC work. They want a tool that does this L1 workflow properly and safely, both to learn the domain and as a portfolio piece that shows sound analyst judgement.

## Solution

A command-line tool that takes one raw `.eml` file and performs a Triage. It extracts the email's Observables, makes Reputation Lookups against Providers (never visiting a URL or opening an attachment), applies red-flag rules to produce Findings, and reaches a Verdict of malicious, suspicious or clean, with a Score and the evidence behind it.

Each Triage produces a saved Triage Report (a structured record that later phases can build on) and an Incident Note the analyst can paste straight into a ticket. The tool is honest about its limits. It shows what it could not check, it never treats Unknown as clean, and it will not give a clean Verdict without the evidence to back it.

The triage logic lives in a core package, and the CLI is a thin wrapper around it, so a later web-based alert queue can reuse the same core.

## User Stories

### Running a Triage

1. As an L1 analyst, I want to run the tool on a single `.eml` file from the command line, so that I can triage a reported email in one step.
2. As an L1 analyst, I want a clear, readable summary in the terminal, so that I can understand the Verdict at a glance.
3. As an L1 analyst, I want to see progress while Reputation Lookups are running, so that I know the tool hasn't frozen while it waits on rate limits.
4. As an L1 analyst, I want the tool to warn me when the file is a Wrapper Email, so that I don't triage a colleague's forwarded report instead of the phish.
5. As an L1 analyst, I want an `--inner` option that triages the email attached inside a Wrapper Email, so that I can analyse the actual phish without extracting it by hand.
6. As an L1 analyst, I want the tool to fail with a clear message if the file isn't a parseable email, so that I'm not given a misleading Verdict on garbage input.

### Extracting Observables

7. As an L1 analyst, I want the From address and display name extracted, so that I can see who the email claims to be from.
8. As an L1 analyst, I want the Reply-To address extracted, so that I can spot replies being diverted elsewhere.
9. As an L1 analyst, I want the full Received chain shown hop by hop, so that I can follow the email's route.
10. As an L1 analyst, I want the Claimed Origin identified and clearly labelled unverified, so that I don't over-trust a header the attacker may have forged.
11. As an analyst in a real deployment, I want to configure Trusted Relays, so that the tool can identify the first hop added by a server I trust.
12. As an L1 analyst, I want the SPF, DKIM and DMARC results read from the recorded Authentication-Results, so that I see what the receiving server decided at delivery time.
13. As an L1 analyst, I want a missing Authentication-Results header reported as "not recorded", not "fail", so that I don't confuse missing data with a failed check.
14. As an L1 analyst, I want every URL in the plain-text and HTML bodies extracted, so that no link is missed.
15. As an L1 analyst, I want defanged URLs, HTML-entity-encoded URLs and SafeLinks-style wrapped URLs decoded offline, so that obfuscated links are analysed as their real destinations.
16. As an L1 analyst, I want shortened URLs recognised as shortened, so that I know their real destination is hidden.
17. As an L1 analyst, I want each attachment's filename, declared type, size and hashes (SHA-256, plus MD5 and SHA-1 for Providers that use them) listed, so that I can look them up and quote them in a ticket.
18. As an L1 analyst, I want attachments hashed whole and never unpacked or opened, so that nothing malicious is ever processed beyond reading its bytes.

### Reputation Lookups

19. As an L1 analyst, I want URLs, domains, the Claimed Origin IP and attachment hashes looked up against VirusTotal, URLhaus, AbuseIPDB and RDAP as appropriate, so that I don't have to paste each one into each site by hand.
20. As an L1 analyst, I want the tool to only look up what Providers already know and never submit anything for scanning, so that no Provider visits the attacker's link on my behalf.
21. As an L1 analyst, I want recipient addresses, subject lines and body text never sent to any Provider, so that the tool doesn't reveal who was targeted.
22. As an L1 analyst, I want a Provider having no record of an Observable shown as Unknown, so that I never mistake "never seen" for "known safe".
23. As an L1 analyst, I want lookups that didn't happen shown as Not Checked, with the reason, so that I know exactly which evidence is missing.
24. As someone trying the tool without every API key, I want it to run anyway and mark the missing Provider's lookups as Not Checked, so that I can still use it.
25. As an L1 analyst, I want duplicate Observables looked up only once, so that rate limits aren't wasted.
26. As an L1 analyst, I want domains looked up before individual URLs, and URL lookups capped at a configurable limit (10 by default), so that a link-heavy email finishes in reasonable time.
27. As an L1 analyst, I want URLs over the cap marked Not Checked, so that the cap is visible and can't produce a false clean.
28. As an L1 analyst, I want the tool to respect each Provider's rate limits by waiting rather than failing, so that lookups succeed on free-tier keys.
29. As an L1 analyst, I want Reputation Lookup results cached, so that re-running a sample doesn't use up my daily quota.
30. As an L1 analyst, I want cached malicious results kept for 7 days and cached Unknown or clean results for only 24 hours, so that a newly flagged phishing URL isn't hidden by a stale cache entry.
31. As an L1 analyst, I want a `--no-cache` option, so that I can force fresh lookups when I need them.
32. As an L1 analyst, I want each domain's registration age looked up via RDAP, so that newly registered domains can be flagged.
33. As an L1 analyst, I want a hidden registration date treated as "unknown age", not "old", so that hidden data doesn't make a domain look trustworthy.

### Findings

34. As an L1 analyst, I want a Finding when the Reply-To domain differs from the From domain, so that I can spot diverted replies.
35. As an L1 analyst, I want a Finding when the display name claims a Protected brand but the sending domain isn't theirs, so that I can spot impersonation.
36. As an L1 analyst, I want a Finding when the sender domain or a link domain is a Lookalike Domain of a Protected Domain, so that I can spot typosquatting.
37. As an L1 analyst, I want the Protected Domains list to be editable, so that I can add my organisation's own domains and the brands relevant to us.
38. As an L1 analyst, I want Findings for DMARC, SPF and DKIM failures, so that authentication problems count towards the Verdict.
39. As an L1 analyst, I want a Finding when a domain was registered in the last 30 days (configurable), so that freshly created phishing infrastructure stands out.
40. As an L1 analyst, I want a Finding when the email uses urgency language, so that pressure tactics count towards the Verdict.
41. As an L1 analyst, I want the urgency phrases kept in an editable list, so that I can tune them without changing code.
42. As an L1 analyst, I want a Finding when a URL shortener is used, so that hidden destinations count towards the Verdict.
43. As an L1 analyst, I want Findings for risky extensions, double extensions (such as `.pdf.exe`), archives and password-protected attachments, so that dangerous attachments are flagged without being opened.
44. As an L1 analyst, I want a Finding when an Observable has some VirusTotal detections but fewer than the decisive threshold, so that weak signals still count.
45. As an L1 analyst, I want a Finding when the Claimed Origin IP has a high AbuseIPDB confidence score, so that known-abusive senders count.
46. As an L1 analyst, I want every Finding to show the evidence that triggered it, so that I can verify it and explain it in a ticket.

### Verdict and Score

47. As an L1 analyst, I want a malicious Verdict whenever there's a Decisive Finding (an attachment hash or URL flagged by 3 or more VirusTotal engines, or a URL or domain listed on URLhaus), so that a confirmed IOC is never outvoted.
48. As an L1 analyst, I want all other Findings to add points to a Score capped at 100, so that I can see how much evidence there is.
49. As an L1 analyst, I want the Score turned into a Verdict by thresholds (0–29 clean, 30–59 suspicious, 60+ malicious), so that Verdicts are consistent between emails.
50. As an L1 analyst, I want the Verdict never to be clean if any URL or attachment was Not Checked, so that missing evidence can't produce false reassurance.
51. As an L1 analyst, I want to be told when the Verdict was capped at suspicious because of missing evidence, so that I know what to check by hand.
52. As the maintainer, I want the Finding weights, thresholds, decisive engine count, URL cap and domain-age limit in a config file, so that I can tune them against the datasets without editing code.

### Triage Report and Incident Note

53. As an L1 analyst, I want each Triage saved as a Triage Report, so that I have a record of what was found and decided.
54. As a future phase (alert queue, blocklist, dashboard), I want each Triage Report to carry a unique report ID, analysis timestamp, tool version, format version, the SHA-256 of the source email and a reserved place for tags, so that old reports can be found, de-duplicated, interpreted and extended.
55. As an L1 analyst, I want an Incident Note generated from the Triage Report, so that I can paste a consistent note into the ticket.
56. As an L1 analyst, I want the Incident Note to open with one line giving the Verdict, Score, sender and subject, so that the next shift can scan it quickly.
57. As an L1 analyst, I want the Incident Note to list the key Findings with their evidence, so that the Verdict is justified in the ticket.
58. As an L1 analyst, I want IOCs in the Incident Note defanged (for example `hxxps://evil[.]com`), so that nobody clicks them from the ticket.
59. As an L1 analyst, I want the Incident Note to state what was Not Checked and why, so that the ticket is honest about gaps.
60. As an L1 analyst, I want Recommended Actions in the Incident Note, chosen from a fixed list based on the Verdict and Findings, so that I have sensible next steps to carry out.
61. As an L1 analyst, I want the tool to only suggest Recommended Actions and never carry them out, so that I stay in control.
62. As someone integrating the tool, I want a `--json` option that prints the Triage Report, so that other tools can consume it.
63. As someone scripting the tool, I want the exit code to reflect the Verdict (0 clean, 1 suspicious, 2 malicious, 3 or higher for errors), so that scripts and the future alert queue can react without parsing text.

### Safety, data and portfolio

64. As the maintainer, I want API keys loaded from a git-ignored `.env` file, with a committed `.env.example`, so that secrets are never committed.
65. As the maintainer, I want public datasets (phishing_pot for phish, SpamAssassin ham for legitimate email) downloaded by a script into a git-ignored folder, so that raw samples with real people's addresses never land in the public repo.
66. As the maintainer, I want to run the tool across the dataset folder and see how many phish and ham emails get each Verdict, so that I can measure false positives and missed phish, and tune the weights.
67. As a portfolio reviewer, I want the safety rules (lookup only, nothing sent beyond attacker-side Observables, Unknown is not clean, clean requires evidence) visible in the docs and behaviour, so that I can see the author's analyst judgement.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Language and tooling:** Python 3.12+, managed with uv, tested with pytest, using a src layout.
- **Core and CLI split:** The triage logic is a core package with one public entry point: it takes the raw email bytes, the settings and a set of Providers, and returns a Triage Report. The core does no printing, no file saving and no reading of environment variables. The CLI is a thin wrapper. It reads the `.eml` file, loads settings and API keys, builds the real Providers, calls the core, prints the terminal view or JSON, saves the Triage Report and sets the exit code.
- **Pipeline stages inside the core:**
  1. Parse the email, or select the inner email when asked.
  2. Extract Observables.
  3. Make Reputation Lookups.
  4. Apply the rules to produce Findings.
  5. Score and reach a Verdict.
  6. Build the Triage Report.
  
  Incident Note generation is a pure function of the Triage Report, meaning it only reads the report and doesn't call out to anything else.
- **Provider interface:** Every Provider has the same small shape. It says which kinds of Observable it handles, and given one Observable it returns a lookup outcome (malicious with a detail such as engine count, suspicious with a detail, clean, Unknown, or Not Checked with a reason) plus raw evidence for the report. Providers are passed in to the core, never created inside it. The real Providers are VirusTotal, URLhaus, AbuseIPDB and RDAP (RDAP returns a registration date or unknown age).
- **Lookup-only rule (ADR 0001):** No code path may fetch a URL, follow a redirect, open or unpack an attachment, or call any Provider endpoint that submits or scans. Only attacker-side Observables are sent to Providers: URLs, domains, the Claimed Origin IP and attachment hashes.
- **Lookup orchestration:**
  - Observables are de-duplicated, and domains are looked up before URLs.
  - URL lookups are capped (default 10). Anything over the cap is Not Checked with the reason "over lookup cap".
  - Each Provider's rate limit is respected by waiting.
  - A missing API key makes that Provider return Not Checked with the reason "no API key". The run continues.
  - A Provider error is also Not Checked with a reason. It is never a crash.
- **Cache:** Reputation Lookup results are cached locally, keyed by Provider and Observable. Malicious results last 7 days, and Unknown or clean results last 24 hours. Not Checked is never cached. The clock is passed in so expiry can be tested. A switch bypasses the cache.
- **Findings:** Each rule is independent. It looks at the parsed email, its Observables and the lookup results, and returns zero or more Findings. Each Finding has a rule identifier, whether it is decisive, its points and human-readable evidence. The urgency rule is keyword and phrase based, behind the same rule interface, so a smarter checker could replace it later.
- **Verdict (ADR 0002):**
  - Any Decisive Finding means malicious.
  - Otherwise, the Score is the sum of the Finding points, capped at 100. The thresholds are 0–29 clean, 30–59 suspicious and 60+ malicious.
  - If any URL or attachment Observable is Not Checked, a clean Verdict is raised to suspicious, and the report records the reason.
- **Default points:**

  | Finding | Points |
  |---|---|
  | Reply-To mismatch | 20 |
  | Display-name brand impersonation | 25 |
  | Lookalike Domain | 30 |
  | DMARC fail | 20 |
  | SPF fail | 10 |
  | DKIM fail | 10 |
  | Domain registered in the last 30 days | 20 |
  | Urgency language | 10 |
  | URL shortener | 10 |
  | Risky, double-extension, archive or password-protected attachment | 25 |
  | VirusTotal detections below the decisive threshold | 15 |
  | High AbuseIPDB confidence on the Claimed Origin | 15 |

  These defaults, the thresholds, the decisive engine count (3), the URL cap (10), the domain-age limit (30 days), the Protected Domains list, the brand names, the urgency phrases, the shortener domains, the risky extensions and the Trusted Relays all live in one settings file.
- **Authentication results** are read from the recorded Authentication-Results header only, never re-checked. Each of SPF, DKIM and DMARC is pass, fail, another recorded value, or not recorded.
- **Received chain:** Parsed into ordered hops. The Claimed Origin is the earliest public IP, or the first hop added by a configured Trusted Relay when there is one. It is labelled unverified unless a Trusted Relay recorded it.
- **URL handling:**
  - URLs are collected from the plain-text and HTML parts.
  - Defanging, HTML entities and SafeLinks-style wrappers are decoded offline as text.
  - Shortener domains are recognised from the settings list. Shortened URLs are looked up as they are, never expanded.
- **Attachments:** Hashed whole (SHA-256, MD5 and SHA-1). The filename, declared type and size are recorded. Archive and password-protection detection uses only what can be read without unpacking (the file type and the zip's encryption flag).
- **Wrapper Emails:** If the email contains an attached email, the Triage Report carries a warning. The inner-email option selects the attached email as the one to triage.
- **Triage Report contents:**
  - report ID
  - analysis timestamp
  - tool version
  - format version (starting at 1)
  - SHA-256 of the source email
  - parsed headers summary
  - Received hops and Claimed Origin
  - authentication results
  - Observables, with their lookup outcomes per Provider
  - Findings
  - Score
  - Verdict, and the reason if it was capped
  - warnings
  - an empty tags list reserved for later ATT&CK mapping

  The format is defined in one place. Phase 1 saves each report as a JSON file in a reports folder, named by report ID.
- **Incident Note:** Plain text in five sections:
  1. Summary line (Verdict, Score, sender, subject)
  2. Key Findings with evidence
  3. Defanged IOCs
  4. Not Checked items and reasons
  5. Recommended Actions, chosen from a fixed list based on the Verdict and which Findings fired
- **CLI:**
  - Takes one positional `.eml` path.
  - Options: inner email, JSON output, no cache.
  - Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 suspicious, 2 malicious, 3 or higher for errors (an unreadable file or an unparseable email).
  - Shows progress during lookups.
- **Secrets:** API keys come only from the environment, via a git-ignored `.env`. A committed `.env.example` lists the variable names. The `.gitignore` covers `.env`, the samples folder, the reports folder, the cache and `.DS_Store`.
- **Datasets:** A script downloads phishing_pot and SpamAssassin ham into the git-ignored samples folder. A separate evaluation command runs the core across a folder and prints Verdict counts for phish and for ham.

## Testing Decisions

- **What makes a good test here:** Tests check external behaviour through the highest seam: given this email, these Provider answers and these settings, the Triage Report has this Verdict, these Findings, these Not Checked entries and this Incident Note content. Tests never call internal helpers directly or assert on internal data structures, so the inside can be reorganised freely.
- **Seam 1, the core entry point (most tests):**
  - Fixture `.eml` files plus fake Providers with canned answers. Areas covered:
    - each rule firing and not firing
    - Decisive Findings overriding the Score
    - the threshold boundaries (29/30 and 59/60)
    - Score capping
    - clean requires evidence
    - Unknown vs Not Checked
    - missing API keys
    - Provider errors
    - de-duplication
    - the URL cap
    - domains being looked up before URLs
    - offline URL decoding (defanged text, entities, SafeLinks)
    - shortened URLs never being expanded
    - attachment hashing and the attachment Findings
    - Authentication-Results parsing, including "not recorded"
    - Received-chain Claimed Origin, with and without Trusted Relays
    - Wrapper Email detection and inner selection
    - all Triage Report metadata fields
    - Incident Note sections, including defanged IOCs and Recommended Actions
  - Fake Providers count their calls (for the cache, de-duplication and cap tests) and can fail on demand (for the Not Checked tests).
  - A fake clock tests cache expiry: malicious lasts 7 days, Unknown and clean last 24 hours, and Not Checked is never cached.
  - A privacy test checks that fake Providers never receive recipient addresses, subject text or body text.
  - A safety test checks that no Provider is ever asked to submit or scan anything.
- **Seam 2, the CLI (a few tests):** Run with fake Providers. These check only the exit codes per Verdict and for errors, the JSON output matching the Triage Report, the inner-email option, the saved report file, and the clear error for an unparseable file. No rule logic is re-tested at this seam.
- **No network in any automated test.** Real Providers are not exercised by the test suite. Their response parsing is tested against saved real response bodies (fixtures) fed through a fake transport, to keep the real Provider code honest.
- **Fixtures:** A handful of small, hand-checked `.eml` samples, with recipient details replaced, are committed. The raw datasets are never committed.
- **Prior art:** None. This is a new codebase, and these tests set the pattern.

## Out of Scope

- Alert queue, web UI and dashboard (later phases will wrap the same core).
- MITRE ATT&CK mapping (the Triage Report reserves an empty tags list for it).
- Case notes, escalation and Recommended Actions being carried out automatically.
- Indicator blocklist (it will be built from IOCs only).
- Trends dashboard and any database storage (Phase 1 uses JSON files; moving to SQLite would be recorded in a later ADR).
- Expanding shortened URLs, by request or through a shortener's API.
- Unpacking archives or hashing files inside them.
- Submitting anything to any Provider for scanning.
- Re-checking SPF, DKIM or DMARC with live DNS.
- LLM-based urgency detection.
- Processing more than one email per CLI run (apart from the evaluation command over a dataset folder).
- Testing on real work emails.

## Further Notes

- The domain vocabulary is defined in `GLOSSARY.md`. Use its terms in code names, output text and tests.
- ADR 0001 (reputation lookups only) and ADR 0002 (points plus Decisive Findings) constrain this work. Any change that conflicts with them should be raised, not silently made.
- The default weights are a starting point. Tuning them against phishing_pot and SpamAssassin ham, and recording the false-positive rate before and after, is part of the portfolio story.
- Per the maintainer's global conventions, the first code change should also create `README.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` (with a Mermaid diagram) and `docs/CONCEPTS.md`.

items.title: Feature request: automatic self-signed macOS code signing for local development builds

labels.name: maintainer-review
labels.description: Requires maintainer review before any action is taken

items.body:
## What

Add an opt-in macOS local-development signing workflow that automatically runs `codesign` on `AetherSDR.app` after a build, using a persistent, developer-local self-signed code-signing certificate.

The goal is to approve macOS consent dialogs once and retain those approvals across normal edit/build/run cycles, rather than being asked again after every rebuild. This should work without requiring a paid Apple Developer membership or access to the project's release-signing credentials.

## Why

Local development currently involves repeated macOS consent boxes after rebuilding the app, even when the developer already granted access. This interrupts testing and makes repeated launches unnecessarily tedious.

Apple documents that unsigned and ad-hoc-signed code cannot maintain a reliable identity across versions: an ad-hoc designated requirement is tied to that particular build. A stable signing identity and compatible designated requirement are therefore the proposed approach; which consent dialogs this resolves must be verified on macOS. See [TN3127: Inside Code Signing: Requirements](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3127-inside-code-signing-requirements).

## Suggested implementation

- Document a one-time setup for a reusable self-signed **Code Signing** certificate in the developer's Keychain. Reuse the identity on subsequent builds instead of generating a certificate each time. Apple's [Code Signing Tasks](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Security/Conceptual/CodeSigningGuide/Procedures/Procedures.html) describes self-signed identities.
- Add a local CMake setting for the signing identity and automatically sign the completed app bundle after build/resource/deployment steps that change its contents.
- Keep the app's bundle identifier and designated requirement compatible across rebuilds, and correctly sign any embedded code in the development bundle.
- Provide actionable errors when signing is explicitly enabled but the selected identity is unavailable or signing fails.
- Keep the option local and opt-in, with private keys outside the repository. Preserve the existing release-signing/notarization workflow.

## Acceptance criteria

- A documented setup enables automatic signing through the normal incremental macOS build workflow.
- Signature verification succeeds, and the signing identity/designated requirement remain compatible after changing source and rebuilding.
- On a real Mac, grant the affected permissions, then rebuild and relaunch at least twice. Record the exact consent dialogs and macOS version, and verify that those grants survive rebuilds with the same identity. Check privacy consent and Keychain access separately where applicable.
- Initial consent and intentional permission revocation still work normally; the workflow preserves approvals through stable identity rather than modifying macOS consent databases or disabling security controls.
- Document any prompts that still recur and any one-time reauthorization needed when switching from an existing unsigned/ad-hoc build to the development identity.

## Request preparation

- [x] Used an AI assistant to structure this request.
- [x] Checked existing issues for a matching signing request.

### Why
BST administrators need a clear way to finish their first Beratungsstelle and create more in their own Träger when explicitly permitted. Re-entering shared information is tedious. Frank wants a mobile-friendly design before production work.

### What to build
A clickable Storybook proposal based on the specification in [Admin1026](https://github.com/OpenResilienceInitiative/ORISO-Admin/issues/1026): invitation permission on/off, full setup after active 2FA, first-centre save, another-or-finish question, copy-block checkbox dialog, editable prefill and repeated centre creation. Reuse the existing general-information form/design system. The proposal supports one or several permitted topics per centre.

Address reuse is confirmed; contacts, opening hours and topic selections are proposed blocks, with initial defaults still for design review. Mock clients must be clearly labelled. Do not implement live grants, new contracts or centre creation in this design task.

### Acceptance
- [ ] Click through centre1 → save → another → select copied blocks → override values → save → finish, including permission off, empty-copy, cancel and save error states.
- [ ] Show mobile390x844, tablet820x1180 and desktop1440x900; additionally check320/412 widths, long DE/EN labels, keyboard/focus and touch.
- [ ] Source-centre identity, staff/permissions/legal approvals and publication state are never copied; the invited first centre is not duplicated.
- [ ] Publish captioned screenshots and show them directly in chat. Record Frank's design feedback before production implementation.

### Reviewer test plan
- [ ] Compare grant on/off → only the granted actor sees additional-centre creation, while both can complete the first authorised centre.
- [ ] Select only address, change the city in the new form and cancel/retry → source details stay unchanged and user edits remain clear.

## Problem Statement

Researchers face severe friction across disjointed tools: discovering high-impact papers across academic search engines (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex), handling paywalled papers requiring university library access (such as UCL SSO), managing references in Zotero, feeding full-text PDFs into AI notebooks (Google NotebookLM) for source-grounded reasoning, and consolidating distilled takeaways into personal knowledge management systems (Obsidian PKM). Manual copy-pasting across these silos is tedious, prone to missing breakthrough reviews, and breaks knowledge permanence.

## Solution

A unified, modular Python & CLI research toolkit with Docker containerization support that automates the end-to-end literature lifecycle while respecting real-world human checkpoints:
1. Multi-source retrieval & composite ranking (Semantic Scholar + OpenAlex), prioritizing review papers and journal impact metrics.
2. Direct insertion into personal Zotero collections with a staged `FulltextCheckpoint` that automatically resolves Open Access PDFs and generates UCL EZproxy links for paywalled papers, seamlessly reconciling Zotero Connector duplicates.
3. Resilient `NotebookLMGateway` (via `notebooklm-py` and Gemini fallback) to sync PDFs and execute source-grounded queries with verbatim citation extraction.
4. Obsidian PKM exporter producing standardized `paper-screen.md` cards in `10-wiki/References/papers/` and candidate knowledge packets in `90-staging/` adhering to `conversation-memory-protocol.md`.
5. First-class Docker and VPS deployment (`Dockerfile` + `docker-compose.yml`) with environment secrets.

## User Stories

1. As a researcher, I want to search for literature by topic keywords across Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex simultaneously, so that I get comprehensive academic coverage without visiting multiple websites.
2. As a researcher, I want the toolkit to deduplicate papers across S2 and OpenAlex using DOI, ArXiv ID, and fuzzy title matching, so that I do not see redundant entries.
3. As a researcher, I want search results to be ranked using a composite score combining age-adjusted citation velocity, journal impact factor (2-year citedness), and relevance, so that landmark and high-quality papers surface to the top regardless of publication year.
4. As a researcher, I want high-quality review and survey papers to be prioritized and allocated the top 25-30% slots in my search results, so that I can establish a bird's-eye view of a field before reading narrow empirical studies.
5. As a researcher, I want review paper age to suffer exponential decay penalties, so that decade-old obsolete surveys do not crowd out fresh, state-of-the-art syntheses.
6. As a researcher, I want the filtered top 5-10 papers to be automatically inserted into a dedicated Zotero collection within my personal library, so that my bibliography is organized by research topic.
7. As a researcher, I want the toolkit to strictly operate in my Zotero personal library rather than group libraries, so that AI-automated imports do not pollute shared group archives like `cyber9`.
8. As a researcher, I want open-access PDFs to be automatically discovered and attached to Zotero items, so that I don't have to manually download publicly available papers.
9. As a researcher with university institutional credentials (UCL), I want the toolkit to halt at an explicit `FulltextCheckpoint` when paywalled papers lack PDFs, so that my automated pipeline does not get blocked by university MFA logins.
10. As a researcher, I want the toolkit to generate clickable UCL EZproxy links (`https://libproxy.ucl.ac.uk/login?url=https://doi.org/...`) for all pending paywalled papers, so that I can authenticate in one click.
11. As a researcher, I want the toolkit to automatically cluster and reconcile duplicate items when I import a full-text paper via the browser Zotero Connector, so that my collection keeps the best metadata and the full-text PDF attachment without manual cleanup.
12. As a researcher, I want a `checkpoint` CLI subcommand to view which papers have local PDFs ready and which remain pending, so that I have clear visibility into my collection status.
13. As a researcher, I want to run `sync-notebook --allow-partial` to proceed with available PDFs if certain papers cannot be retrieved, so that my research is not blocked by a single unavailable document.
14. As a researcher, I want the toolkit to scan my local `~/Zotero/storage/<key>/*.pdf` directory directly, so that large PDFs are read instantly without consuming Zotero cloud storage quota.
15. As a researcher, I want the toolkit to create a dedicated notebook in Google NotebookLM and upload all resolved PDFs as sources, so that I can perform grounded reasoning against the entire document corpus.
16. As a researcher, I want to authenticate with NotebookLM using either local Chrome cookies, serialized JSON profiles, or durable Android Master Tokens, so that authentication is seamless on both desktop and remote VPS servers.
17. As a researcher, I want the `NotebookLMGateway` to support an official Google Gemini File API fallback adapter, so that unexpected internal Google RPC shifts never break my research workflow.
18. As a researcher, I want to execute grounded Q&A queries against my NotebookLM sources via the CLI, so that I can synthesize findings, compare methodologies, and extract key claims.
19. As a researcher, I want NotebookLM answers to return verbatim cited text spans and character offsets, so that every claim is anchored in primary literature evidence.
20. As a researcher, I want the toolkit to generate screening paper notes (`paper-screen.md`) in `/home/ling/vault/PKM/10-wiki/References/papers/YYYY-FirstAuthor-ShortTitle.md`, so that new papers immediately enter my permanent knowledge vault.
21. As a researcher, I want paper notes to contain direct desktop deep links (`zotero://select/users/<id>/items/<key>` and `zotero://open-pdf/users/<id>/items/<pdf_key>`), so that I can jump directly to the paper in Zotero from Obsidian.
22. As a researcher, I want synthesized evidence and findings from NotebookLM to be exported to `/home/ling/vault/PKM/90-staging/<slug>.md` using the `memory-candidate.md` template, so that AI-generated insights are held as staging candidates before formal promotion.
23. As a researcher, I want to pass an optional `--project <slug>` parameter to link paper notes and candidate memories to my Obsidian project pages (`30-projects/<slug>/project-overview.md`), so that my reading directly enriches active manuscripts.
24. As a researcher, I want every Obsidian vault export to append an audit line to `/home/ling/vault/PKM/log.md`, so that my background `obsidian-sync.service` preserves an intelligible change history.
25. As a researcher, I want the entire toolkit to be containerized via `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml`, so that I can ship it to my remote Linux VPS and run long-running research tasks with zero environment drift.
26. As a researcher, I want all sensitive credentials (API keys, session tokens, user IDs) to be loaded from a `.env` file, so that no secrets are committed to Git.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Domain Model**: Strictly conforms to `CONTEXT.md` vocabulary (`PaperCandidate`, `ReviewPaper`, `Ranker`, `ZoteroCollection`, `FulltextCheckpoint`, `NotebookLMGateway`, `NotebookSource`, `DistilledEvidence`).
- **Retrieval & Deduplication**: Multi-source client for Semantic Scholar (1 RPS throttled) and OpenAlex (abstract reconstruction from inverted index). Deduplication uses 3-tier cascade: canonical DOI -> ArXiv ID -> Fuzzy title similarity (>= 0.90 within 1 year).
- **Ranking Formulation**: $Score(p) = 0.40 S_{rel}(p) + 0.35 S_{cite}(p) + 0.25 S_{venue}(p) + B_{review}(p)$. Uses OpenAlex 2-year citedness as JCR IF proxy and exponential decay for review age. Stratified selection guarantees top 25-30% slots for leading review papers.
- **Zotero & FulltextCheckpoint**: Hybrid pattern recorded in **ADR-0001**. Writes collections and metadata via Web API (`pyzotero`); probes local disk `~/Zotero/storage/<key>/*.pdf` for 0-quota PDF paths. Halts on missing paywalled papers with clickable UCL EZproxy links (`https://libproxy.ucl.ac.uk/login?url=https://doi.org/{doi}`) and clusters Connector duplicates by DOI.
- **Personal Library Isolation**: Recorded in **ADR-0002**. All AI Zotero operations and URI schemes target `users/<user_id>` exclusively, preventing interference with group libraries like `cyber9`.
- **NotebookLM Gateway**: Protocol-driven `NotebookLMGateway` supporting primary adapter `NotebookLMPyAdapter` (`teng-lin/notebooklm-py`) with dual-mode auth (Chrome cookies / Android Master Token) and fallback adapter `GeminiGroundingFallbackAdapter` using official Google GenAI File API.
- **Obsidian PKM Integration**: Conforms to `50-meta/conversation-memory-protocol.md`. Exports `paper-screen.md` cards to `10-wiki/References/papers/YYYY-FirstAuthor-ShortTitle.md` and candidate evidence packets to `90-staging/<slug>.md`. Automatically updates `/home/ling/vault/PKM/log.md`.
- **Packaging & VPS Deployment**: Recorded in **ADR-0003**. `Dockerfile` based on `python:3.11-slim`, `docker-compose.yml` with persistent volumes (`./data:/app/data`, `toolkit-cache`), and `.env.example`.

## Testing Decisions

- **Testing Philosophy**: Test external observable behavior and contract boundaries, minimizing mock brittleness.
- **Seam 1: High-Level CLI Workflow Seam**: The highest integration seam (`research_toolkit.cli` / `workflow.py`). Tested against mocked HTTP transports for S2, OpenAlex, Zotero, and NotebookLM, verifying correct state transitions across `search`, `checkpoint`, `sync-notebook`, and `ask`.
- **Seam 2: Algorithmic Seam (Ranker & Deduplication)**: Pure function tests without network I/O. Verifies exact composite scores, edge cases (missing DOI, zero citations, preprints), and review quota guarantees.
- **Seam 3: PKM Exporter Seam**: File serialization tests verifying correct Markdown frontmatter, slugified filenames (`YYYY-FirstAuthor-ShortTitle.md`), personal Zotero URI schemes, and audit log appending.

## Out of Scope

- Developing a GUI or web frontend (CLI and containerized MCP server suffice).
- Automated scraping bypassing university MFA/SSO (deliberately delegated to the human at FulltextCheckpoint).
- Custom cloud synchronization backends (relies on native Zotero sync and Obsidian sync service).

## Further Notes

- Prototype simulation already validated on `main` at `docs/prototypes/workflow-checkpoint-demo.html` and `scripts/prototype_cli.py`.
